[Homage]
Having duly revered the composer of this treatise, the son of the Well-Gone One (<s>Sugata</s>), I shall endeavor, for speakers beginning from ourselves, in the discrimination of the meaning,
3:
[Body of the Treatise]
Here, to begin with, the body of the treatise is established,
4: For definition, indeed, is the characteristic; the reality; the cultivation of the antidote,
5: And herein also the stages, attainment of the result, and the unsurpassed of the vehicles as well,
6: Thus these seven topics in this treatise are taught: that is to say, definition; obscuration; reality; the cultivation of the antidote; and precisely within that cultivation of the antidote, the stages; and attainment of the result; and the unsurpassedness of the vehicles as the seventh topic,
7:
[CHAPTER I. Section on Definitions]
[1. <s>Abhūtaparikalpa</s> (imaginary construction); a. the mark of existent and non-existent]
Thereupon, beginning with the definition, he states:
8: <s>Abhūtaparikalpa</s> (imaginary construction) exists; duality is not found there, emptiness is indeed found here, and even within that it is found, 1.1
10: Here, <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> is the conceptual construction of grasped and grasper; the duality is the grasped and the grasper; emptiness is the absence, with respect to that <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, of the status of grasped and grasper; even within that, it is found—this is <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>. In this way, he sees in accordance with reality that whatever is not present in a given locus makes that locus empty by that [absence], and he understands in accordance with reality that whatever remains here is truly present—thus the unperverted mark of emptiness is brought to light,
11: It is not empty, nor is it non-empty; therefore everything is designated; from existence, from non-existence, and from existence—this is the middle approach, I.2
12: It is not empty—neither by emptiness nor by <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>; nor is it non-empty—by the duality of grasped and grasper. Everything conditioned is what is termed <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, and the unconditioned is what is termed emptiness; it is designated—pointed out—on account of existence, of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>; of non-existence, of duality; and of existence, of emptiness, within <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, and of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> within that—this is the middle approach with respect to all things: not exclusively empty, not exclusively non-empty. In this way, this reading is harmonized with the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> and similar texts: “All this is not empty, nor again non-empty,”
13:
[b. Own-characteristic]
Having thus made known the existent and non-existent marks of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, he makes known its own-characteristic,
14: A seeming of object, existence, self, and cognition arises; and the cognition does not have that object, because of the absence of that—hence that too is non-existent, I.3
15: Here, “seeming of object” is what appears in the mode of form and so on; “seeming of existence” is the presentation as the five senses in one’s own and others’ streams; “seeming of self” is the afflicted mind, owing to conjunction with self-delusion and the like; “seeming of cognition” is the six cognitions. “And the cognition does not have that object,” for the “object/existence/self/cognition”-seeming lacks true form, and the seeming of self and cognition is false-seeming,
17: Thus, “because of the absence of that, that too is non-existent”: since what is grasped—form, the five senses, and mind—and what is termed the six cognitions are fourfold, because of the absence of that grasped object, that which grasps, cognition, is also non-existent,
18: Therefore, for this, the status of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> is established; yet not so as absolute non-existence,
19: Because its being is not as it appears when it arises, nor is there absolute non-existence, since mere error does arise; why then is sheer non-existence of it not to be asserted? Because
20: Liberation is taught as from its cessation, I.4
21: Otherwise, neither bondage nor liberation would be established—there would be the fault of denying both defilement and purification,
22:
[c. Collecting-characteristic]
Having thus made known the own-characteristic of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, he makes known the collecting-characteristic—how, when there is mere <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, the collection of the three natures is obtained,
23: The imagined, the dependent, and indeed the perfectly accomplished are taught from the standpoint of the meaning, from <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> (imaginary construction), and from the absence of duality, I.5
24: The “meaning” is the <s>parikalpita</s> (imagined) own-nature; <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> is the <s>paratantra</s> (dependent) own-nature; the absence of grasper and grasped is the <s>pariniṣpanna</s> (perfectly accomplished) own-nature,
25:
[d. Mark of the means of entry into the non-real characteristic]
Now, with respect to that very <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, he elucidates the mark of the means for entering the non-real characteristic,
27: Relying upon apprehension, non-apprehension arises; relying upon non-apprehension, non-apprehension arises, I.6
28: Relying upon apprehension as mere <s>vijñapti</s> (representation), non-apprehension of objects arises; relying upon non-apprehension of objects, even non-apprehension of mere <s>vijñapti</s> arises; in this way the non-real characteristic enters into grasper and grasped,
29: From apprehension, then, the nature of non-apprehension is established,
30: Because, in the absence of an object to be apprehended, apprehension is inapplicable,
31: And from this, the equality of non-apprehension and apprehension is to be understood, I.7
32: Because apprehension, as apprehension, is not established, yet apprehension is said to be of the nature of non-apprehension, inasmuch as it appears as an unreal object,
33:
[e. Mark of division]
Now he makes known the mark of division of that very <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>,
34: And <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> is mind and mental factors, within the three realms,
35: By the division into the <s>Kāma</s>, <s>Rūpa</s>, and <s>Ārūpya</s> spheres,
36:
[f. Mark by synonym]
And he makes known the mark by synonym,
37: Therein, the cognition is the seeing of the mere object, while, with respect to the specification of that, the mental factors, I.8
38: There, the seeing with regard to the mere object is cognition; the seeing with regard to the specified object is the mental factors—feeling and the rest,
39:
[g. Mark of functioning]
And he makes known the mark of functioning,
41: One is the condition-cognition; the second is for enjoyment; and there, the mental factors impel delimitation and enjoyment, I.9
42: <s>Ālayavijñāna</s> (storehouse-cognition), being the condition of the other cognitions, is the condition-cognition; the cognition that has that as its condition is the functioning cognition, for enjoyment; enjoyment is feeling; delimitation is conception; the impellers are formations—intention, attention, and the like of cognition,
43:
[h. Mark of affliction]
And he makes known the mark of affliction,
44: By covering and by planting, and by leading and by appropriation, by filling, by triple delimitation, by enjoyment, and by dragging, I.10
45: By binding and by directing-toward, and by suffering, the world is afflicted,
46: Therein, by covering is meant the fettering of seeing-as-it-is by ignorance; by planting, the establishing of the karmic latencies of action in cognition through formations; by leading, the bringing of a being by cognition to the place of re-arising; by appropriation, the embodied complex through name-and-form; by filling, by the six sense-bases; by triple delimitation, by contact; by enjoyment, by feeling; by dragging, by craving, of the future existence propelled by action; by binding, by the appropriations, whereby cognition is bound to objects such as desire that are conducive to its arising; by directing-toward, the orienting of action done in existence (<s>bhava</s>) toward giving its maturation in a future existence; by suffering, the world is tormented by birth and by aging-and-death; thus this
47: Affliction is threefold and twofold, on account of imaginary construction it is sevenfold, I.11
48: Affliction is threefold: affliction as defilements; affliction as actions; and affliction as birth. Therein, affliction as defilements is ignorance, craving, and appropriation; affliction as actions is formations and existence (<s>bhava</s>); affliction as birth is the remaining factors. Affliction is twofold: affliction as cause and affliction as result,
50: Therein, affliction as cause, with the limbs whose nature is defilements and actions; and affliction as result, with the remaining [limbs]; affliction is sevenfold; the cause is sevenfold: the cause as inversion (<s>viparyāsahetu</s>); the cause as impelling (<s>ākṣepahetu</s>); the cause as bringing-in (<s>upanayahetu</s>); the cause as appropriation (<s>parigrahahetu</s>); the cause as enjoyment (<s>upabhogahetu</s>); the cause as drawing-in (<s>ākarṣaṇahetu</s>); and the cause as agitation (<s>udvegahetu</s>); therein, the cause as inversion is ignorance; the cause as impelling is formations; the cause as bringing-in is cognition; the cause as appropriation is name-and-form and the six sense-bases; the cause as enjoyment is contact and feeling; the cause as drawing-in is craving, appropriation, and existence (<s>bhava</s>); the cause as agitation is birth, aging, and death; and all this affliction proceeds from <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> (imaginary construction),
51:
[Summary meaning of <s>Abhūtaparikalpa</s>]
As for the summary meaning, the ninefold characteristic of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> is made clear: the mark of the existent; the mark of the non-existent; the own-characteristic; the collecting-characteristic; the mark of the means of entry into the non-real characteristic; the mark of division; the mark by synonym; the mark of functioning; and the mark of affliction,
52:
[2. <s>Śūnyatā</s> (emptiness)]
Having thus made known <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s>, he indicates how <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) is to be understood,
53: The characteristic, and then the synonyms; its meaning; and the division as well; and the means [of realization]—such, in brief, is to be understood for <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness), I.12
54:
[a. The characteristic of <s>Śūnyatā</s>]
How is the characteristic to be understood?
55: The absence of duality, indeed the existence of absence—this is the characteristic of the empty,
56: The absence of duality—of grasper and grasped; and the existence of that absence, as emptiness,
58: —is the characteristic; thus the being-a-mark of an absence-nature is made clear for <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness); and that very absence-nature is such that
59: It is not existence, nor indeed non-existence,
60: How is it not existence? Because it is the absence of duality; how is it not non-existence? Because it is the existence of the absence of duality; and this is the characteristic of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness); therefore, of <s>abhūtaparikalpa</s> (imaginary construction),
61: there is neither the characteristic of difference nor of identity, I.13
62: If there were difference, it would not be fitting to say, “Dharma is other than <s>dharma</s>” (the quality is other than the qualified); as with impermanence and suffering; if there were identity, the knowledge whose object is purification would not exist, nor the general characteristic; by this, a characteristic free from “is” and “is-other” is made clear,
63:
[b. The synonyms of <s>Śūnyatā</s>]
How are the synonyms to be understood?
64: <s>Tathatā</s> (suchness), and the limit of reality (<s>bhūtakoṭi</s>), and the signless (<s>ānimitta</s>), and the ultimate truth (<s>paramārthatā</s>), and the <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of phenomena) are, in brief, synonyms of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness), I.14
65:
[c. The meaning of the synonyms of <s>Śūnyatā</s>]
How is the meaning of the synonyms to be understood?
66: By the meanings of “not otherwise,” “free from inversion,” “cessation of signs,” “the Arya-domain,” and because of being the cause of the noble qualities—such, in order, is the meaning of the synonyms, I.15
67: By the meaning “not otherwise,” <s>Tathatā</s> (suchness), since it is perpetual as just thus; by the meaning “free from inversion,” the limit of reality (<s>bhūtakoṭi</s>), because inversions are unreal; by the meaning of cessation of signs, the signless (<s>ānimitta</s>), because of the absence of all signs; because it is the domain of noble knowledge, the ultimate truth (<s>paramārtha</s>), since it is the object of supreme knowledge; and because it is the cause of noble qualities, the <s>dharmadhātu</s>,
69: —because the noble qualities arise having that as their object; here, the meaning of “cause” is the meaning of “source/element” (<s>dhātu</s>),
70:
[d. The divisions of <s>Śūnyatā</s>]
How is the division of <s>śūnyatā</s> to be known?
71: It is defiled, and it is pure,
72: —such is its division; in which condition is it defiled, and in which pure?
73: It is with stains, and without stains,
74: When it operates together with stain, then it is defiled; when the stains are abandoned, then it is pure; if, being with stains, it becomes without stains, how is it that, as a bearer of alteration, it does not become impermanent? Because for it
75: purity is accepted like the clarity of water, of gold, and of space, I.1
76: the removal of adventitious defilements does not constitute an other-nature of it,
78: This is another division: the sixteenfold <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness)—<s>adhyātmaśūnyatā</s> (internal-emptiness), <s>bahirdhāśūnyatā</s> (external-emptiness), <s>adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā</s> (internal-and-external-emptiness), <s>mahāśūnyatā</s> (great-emptiness), <s>śūnyatāśūnyatā</s> (emptiness-of-emptiness), <s>paramārthaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness as ultimate), <s>saṃskṛtaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of the conditioned), <s>asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of the unconditioned), <s>atyantaśūnyatā</s> (utter-emptiness), <s>anavarāgraśūnyatā</s> (beginning-and-endless-emptiness), <s>anavakāraśūnyatā</s> (non-diminishing-emptiness), <s>prakṛtiśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of nature), <s>lakṣaṇaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of characteristics), <s>sarvadharmaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of all phenomena), <s>abhāvaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of non-existence), and <s>abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā</s> (emptiness of the nature-of-non-existence); this, in summary, is to be understood,
79: Emptiness of enjoyer, of what is enjoyed, and of the support-body of those; and that which, however, is seen—by whom, how, and for what purpose—of that there is emptiness, I.17
80: Therein, emptiness of the enjoyer is the internal sense-bases; emptiness of what is enjoyed is the external ones; the body of those two—the enjoyer and what is enjoyed—the basis, the body, of that there is emptiness, and this is called internal-and-external-emptiness; the supporting-thing is the receptacle-world; because of its vastness, its emptiness is called great-emptiness; and that internal sense-bases and the like, by which it is seen as empty—by knowledge of emptiness—of that there is emptiness, [namely] emptiness-of-emptiness; and as it is seen in the mode of the ultimate, of that there is emptiness, [namely] emptiness as ultimate; and for the sake of which the <s>bodhisattva</s> undertakes [it], of that too there is emptiness; and for what purpose does he undertake [it]?
81: For the attainment of the twofold auspicious,
82: Of the wholesome conditioned and unconditioned,
83: And always for the welfare of beings,
84: For the sake of the utmost welfare of beings,
85: And for the purpose of abandoning <s>saṃsāra</s>,
86: For, not seeing the emptiness of beginning-and-endless <s>saṃsāra</s>, one would grow weary and abandon <s>saṃsāra</s>,
87: And for the inexhaustibility of the wholesome, I.18
88: And even in <s>nirvāṇa</s> with no residue of substratum, that which neither scatters nor discards—of that there is emptiness,
91: And for the purification of the lineage (<s>gotra</s>),
92: For lineage indeed is nature, since it is intrinsic,
93: For the acquisition of marks and secondary signs,
94: For the attainment of the marks of a Great Person together with the secondary signs,
95: For the purification of the Buddha-qualities does the <s>bodhisattva</s> undertake [it], I.19
96: Such are, thus far, the established accounts of fourteen emptinesses; what, then, here is emptiness?
97: Emptiness here is the non-existence of the person or of phenomena; and the existence of that non-existence—therein, that is the other emptiness, I.20
98: The non-existence of person and phenomena is emptiness; and the existence of that non-existence—therein, with respect to the aforesaid enjoyer and so on—this is another emptiness; in order to make known the characteristic of emptiness, he establishes, at the end, a twofold emptiness: emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of the nature-of-non-existence, respectively, for the avoidance of the superimposition of person-and-phenomena and of the negation of that emptiness; thus the division of emptiness is to be understood,
99:
[e. The means of realizing <s>śūnyatā</s>]
How is the means to be understood?
100: If it were defiled, then all embodied beings would be freed; if it were purified, then exertion would be fruitless, I.21
103: If the emptiness of phenomena, even when adventitious afflictions have not arisen because of a counteragent, were not defiled—because of the absence of defilement—then all beings would become liberated effortlessly; and if, even when a counteragent has arisen, it were not purified, then the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be fruitless; and having thus determined,
104: It is neither defiled nor not-defiled, neither pure nor impure as such,
105: How is it not defiled, nor impure? By very nature,
106: Because of the luminousness of mind,
107: How is it not undefiled, nor pure?
109: In this way, the division of emptiness that was set forth is established
110:
[Summary-meaning of <s>Śūnyatā</s> (emptiness)]
Therein, the summary-meaning of <s>śūnyatā</s> is to be understood by way of definition and by way of establishment; therein, by way of definition, by the characteristic of non-existence and by the characteristic of existence; and again, the “existence-characteristic” is by the characteristic of being free from existence-and-non-existence, and by the characteristic of being free from identity-and-otherness; again, establishment is to be understood by the establishment beginning with synonyms; here, by this fourfold manner of exposition, there are brought to light the own-characteristic of <s>śūnyatā</s>, the action-characteristic, the characteristic of affliction-and-purification, and the characteristic according to reasoning, for the pacification of conceptualization, fear, sloth, and doubt,
111: In the Madhyāntavibhāga, the delimitation of the non-instant (akṣaṇa) is first,
113:
[CHAPTER II. Delimitation of Obstructions]
[1. The five obstructions beginning with “pervasive”]
115: The avoidance of what is pervasive, particular, excessive, equal, and of appropriation—twofold obstruction is declared,
116: Therein, the pervasive obstruction of afflictions and knowables is, in its entirety, for those of the <s>bodhisattva</s>-lineage; the particular obstruction of afflictions is for those of the <s>śrāvaka</s> and the like lineages; the excessive is for those very ones who are of the character of lust and so on; the equal is for those of equal-share character; the obstruction of appropriation-and-abandonment with respect to <s>saṃsāra</s> is for those of the <s>bodhisattva</s>-lineage, because of the obstruction of non-abiding <s>nirvāṇa</s>; thus, as is fitting, this twofold obstruction is declared for both—for those of the <s>bodhisattva</s>-lineage and for those of the <s>śrāvaka</s> and the like lineages,
117: [2. The obstruction of the nine fetters in the path of practice]
119: Ninefold is the characteristic of affliction, II.1
121: The nine fetters are the obstruction of afflictions; of whom is this obstruction?
122: Of agitation and of equanimity, and of non-seeing of reality,
123: The fetter of indulgence is the obstruction of the zealous; the fetter of aversion is (
125: ) of the equanimous; for by that, he is not able to regard with equanimity even an adverse object of aversion; the remaining are the obstruction of the seeing of reality; how so?—those, in order,
126: With respect to the view of a real person, and of that very object; and with respect to the jewels of cessation and path, and indeed esteem for gains and honors; in the understanding of ascetic refinement, II.2
127: The fetters become an obstruction; for the fetter of conceit, in the discerning of the view of a real person, becomes an obstruction, because at the time of realization, by the force of the inner and intermediary uprisings of the conceit “I am,” that is not abandoned; the fetter of ignorance, in the discerning of the object of the view of a real person, because of the non-discernment of the aggregates of appropriation; the fetter of views, in the discerning of the truth of cessation, because of intimidation by the extremes of eternalism with respect to the person and of annihilationism—thereby—its disparagement by wrong view; the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa), in the discerning of the truth of the path, because of grasping at purification of what is otherwise (than the path); the fetter of doubt, in the discerning of the Three Jewels, because of lack of faith in their qualities; the fetter of envy, in the discerning of gains and honors, because of not seeing their faults; the fetter of stinginess, in the discerning of ascetic refinement, because of fixation on embellishment,
129:
[3. The <s>bodhisattva</s>-obstruction]
[a. The obstruction with respect to the ten virtues and the like]
130: Further, with respect to the wholesome and the like, it is tenfold, II.3
131: Further, another obstruction is to be known, in the tenfold wholesome and the like; what is that obstruction, and what are the wholesome and the like?
132: Non-application; in a wrong sphere; what is effected by improper yoga; non-arising; non-attention; non-fulfillment of the accumulation, II.4
133: Desolation of lineage and of spiritual friend; weariness of mind,
136: And desolation of practice; dwelling among wicked people, II.5
137: Harshness; residual taints; from the three, unripe wisdom,
138: And harshness indeed by nature; sloth; heedlessness, II.6
139: Attachment to becoming and to enjoyments; and mental torpor,
140: Lack of faith; premature certitude; and investigation merely according to what is heard, II.7
141: Disrespect for the true Dharma; heaviness with respect to alms; and miserliness as well; addiction to hearing; littleness (meanness); and ill-preparation for concentration, II.8
142: This is the obstruction; who are the wholesome and the like?
143: The wholesome: awakening; undertaking; intelligence; non-delusion; unobstructedness; absence of haughtiness; fearlessness here; absence of envy; and mastery—these are the wholesome and the like, II.9
144: Regarding these wholesome and the like, he says: of which, how many obstructions are to be known?
145: And indeed, for these, three, three obstructions are to be known,
146: For the wholesome, there are three obstructions: non-application; application in a wrong sphere; and application contrary to method (<s>ayonisaḥ-prayoga</s>) For awakening, three: non-arising of the wholesome; non-attention; and non-fulfillment of the accumulation; undertaking is the arising of <s>bodhicitta</s> For this, three: desolation of lineage (<s>gotra-vaidhurya</s>); desolation of spiritual friend (<s>kalyāṇa-mitra-vaidhurya</s>); and weariness-of-mind For intelligence, [namely] <s>bodhisattva</s>-hood; for its knowledge, three obstructions: desolation of practice (<s>pratipatti-vaidhurya</s>); dwelling among base people; and dwelling among wicked people; therein, a “base person” is a foolish person, [and] a “wicked person” is one obstructive For the unconfused, three: coarseness arising from inversion; the condition of something-or-other remaining from the triad of obstructions beginning with afflictions; and immaturity of the knowledge that ripens liberation; the abandoning of obstruction is non-obstruction; for this, three: innate coarseness; sloth; and heedlessness; for the deflected, three, by which he turns the mind elsewhere, not toward unsurpassed perfect awakening,
148: Attachment to becoming; attachment to enjoyments; and mental torpor; for fearlessness here, three: non-conceivability regarding the person; non-resolution regarding the Dharma; and investigation merely according to what is heard, as to the matter of words For non-miserliness, three: disrespect for the true Dharma; regard for gains, honors, and worship; and lack of compassion toward beings For mastery, three, by which he does not obtain supremacy: addiction to hearing—arising from actions that conduce to addiction to Dharma-hearing; scant learning; and ill-preparation for concentration,
149: [b. The ten causes] Now, again, this obstruction—beginning with the wholesome—is to be understood, with respect to the relevant object, by means of the ten causes wherever there are ten causes; the ten causes are: the cause of arising, such as the eye and the like for eye-consciousness; the cause of abiding, such as the four nourishments for living beings; the cause of support, namely, whatever is the base for something, as, for example, the vessel-world for the world of beings; the cause of manifestation, such as light for visible form; the cause of alteration, such as fire and the like for cooking and the like; the cause of separation, such as a knife and the like for what is to be cut and the like; the cause of transformation, such as goldsmiths and the like for gold and so on in the state of bracelet and the like; the cause of co-conditioning (<s>saṃpratyaya</s>), such as smoke and the like for fire and the like; the cause of making-to-apprehend (<s>saṃpratyāyana</s>), such as a reason (<s>hetu</s>) for a thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>); the cause of attainment, such as the paths and the like for <s>nirvāṇa</s> and so on,
150: Accordingly, the obstruction of arising is to be seen in the wholesome, because it ought to be produced; the obstruction of abiding is [to be seen] in awakening, because it is unshakable; the obstruction of support is [to be seen] in undertaking, because <s>bodhicitta</s> is its support; the obstruction of manifestation is [to be seen] in intelligence, because it is to be made manifest; the obstruction of alteration is [to be seen] in the unconfused, because, being a turning away from confusion, it is an alteration,
152: the obstruction of separation is [to be seen] in non-obstruction, because it is disjunction from obstruction; the obstruction of transformation is [to be seen] in bowing, in awakening, because its characteristic is the transformation of mind; the obstruction of co-conditioning is [to be seen] in fearlessness here, because, through non-co-conditioning, there is trembling; the obstruction of making-to-apprehend is [to be seen] in non-miserliness, because by non-miserliness with respect to the Dharma one causes others to apprehend; the obstruction of attainment is [to be seen] in mastery, because its characteristic is the attainment of supremacy,
153: Cause is tenfold—in arising, abiding, support, manifestation,
154: In alteration, separation, transformation, co-conditioning, making-to-apprehend, and attainment,
155: The eye, nourishment, base, light, fire, and the like—these are their illustrations,
156: Knife, artisan, the knowing of reason, smoke, path, and so on are the others
157: For one who wishes to attain <s>Bodhi</s> (awakening), from the very beginning, a root of the wholesome is to be generated; then, by the strengthening through the power of the root of the wholesome, <s>Bodhi</s> is to be attained; again, for the generation of that very root of the wholesome, there is the establishment of <s>bodhicitta</s> (the thought of awakening); the <s>bodhisattva</s> is the basis (support) of that <s>bodhicitta</s>; therefore, by that <s>bodhisattva</s> who has generated <s>bodhicitta</s> and obtained strengthening by the power of the root of the wholesome, having abandoned inversion (error), non-inversion (correct cognition) is to be generated; thereafter, with non-inversion on the path of seeing (<s>darśanamārga</s>), on the path of cultivation (<s>bhāvanāmārga</s>) all obstructions are to be abandoned; with obstructions abandoned, all roots of the wholesome are to be dedicated toward unsurpassed perfect awakening (<s>anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi</s>); then, by the strengthening of dedication, one should not tremble in profound and exalted teachings of the Dharma; and with mind thus unshaken, seeing the qualities in the Dharmas, those Dharmas are to be thoroughly illuminated to others in detail; then that <s>bodhisattva</s>, thus endowed by the power of diverse qualities, swiftly
159: attains unsurpassed perfect awakening (<s>anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi</s>) and attains mastery over all Dharmas—this is the sequence of the auspicious and the like,
160: [4. Obstruction in the Bodhipakṣa, the Pāramitās, and the Bhūmis]
161: There is, moreover, another obstruction in the bodhipakṣa, the pāramitās, and the bhūmis, II.10
162: [a. Obstruction in the Bodhipakṣas] As to the bodhipakṣas,
163: In the establishments of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>), maladroitness with respect to the object is an obstruction; in right abandonings (<s>samyak-prahāṇa</s>), sloth; in the bases of supernormal potency (<s>ṛddhipāda</s>), the deficiency of concentration in both aspects; and in their fulfillment, from the lack of any one among zeal, vigor, mind, and inquiry; and in cultivation, from the deficiency of the formations of abandoning; in the faculties (<s>indriya</s>), the non-imposition (failure to apply) of those that partake of liberation; in the powers (<s>bala</s>), the weakness of those very faculties, because of scattering by the opponents; in the factors of awakening (<s>bodhyaṅga</s>), the fault of view, because they are empowered by the path of seeing; in the path-factors (<s>mārgāṅga</s>), the fault of coarseness, because they are empowered by the path of cultivation,
165: [b. Obstruction in the Pāramitās] Obstruction in the pāramitās,
167: Obstruction to sovereignty (lordship), and to a good destination of rebirth, and to the non-abandonment of beings,
168: And, in the diminishing and increase of faults and qualities, obstruction to bringing (beings) to maturation, II.12
169: And obstruction in liberation, in inexhaustibility, in non-interruption of the wholesome,
170: In making-determinate, and in the enjoyment and ripening of Dharma, II.13
171: Here, for the ten pāramitās, whatever fruit belongs to whatever pāramitā, that obstruction—by obstructing that (fruit)—becomes manifest as its obstruction; therein, for the perfection of giving (<s>dāna-pāramitā</s>), obstruction is obstruction to sovereignty and lordship; for the perfection of morality (<s>śīla-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to a good destination; for the perfection of patience (<s>kṣānti-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to non-abandonment of beings; for the perfection of vigor (<s>vīrya-pāramitā</s>), obstruction in the diminishing of faults and the increase of qualities; for the perfection of concentration (<s>dhyāna-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to bringing trainees to maturation; for the perfection of wisdom (<s>prajñā-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to liberation; for the perfection of skill in means (<s>upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to the inexhaustibility of giving and so forth; for dedication to awakening (<s>bodhi-pariṇāmanā</s>), because of making that inexhaustible; for the perfection of aspiration (<s>praṇidhāna-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to the continuous engagement of the wholesome in every birth—because, by the power of aspiration, there is the inclusion of a rebirth conducive to that; for the perfection of power (<s>bala-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to making that very wholesome fixed (irreversible), because, without the strengths of discriminative analysis and cultivation (<s>pratisaṃkhyāna-bhāvanā-bala</s>), the adversaries are not overcome; for the perfection of knowledge (<s>jñāna-pāramitā</s>), obstruction to the enjoyment and ripening of Dharma for oneself and others, because of a failure to understand the meaning of what is heard as it truly is,
172: [c. Obstruction in the Bhūmis] In the bhūmis, again, in order,
174: In the meaning of what is all-pervading, in the meaning of what is foremost, and indeed in the meaning of the foremost of outflow (derivation),
175: And in the meaning of non-appropriation, and indeed in the very (meaning of) non-diversity of continuum,
176: And in the meaning of stainless purity, and indeed in the meaning of non-plurality,
177: And in the meaning of non-loss and non-gain, and in the basis of the fourfold mastery,
178: In the <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of Dharma), this ignorance—undefiled, tenfold in its phases; and, by opposition to the ten bhūmis, the bhūmis themselves are the antidotes; in the <s>dharmadhātu</s>, whatever undefiled non-knowledge there is in the tenfold meanings beginning with the all-pervading—this is, in the ten <s>bodhisattva</s>-bhūmis, an obstruction, in order, because of being their opposite; that is to say,
179: In the meaning of what is all-pervading,
180: For, by the first bhūmi indeed, he penetrates the meaning of the <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of Dharma) as all-pervading, by which he attains equality of self and other; by the second, the meaning of what is foremost, by which it is thus for him: “Therefore, then, for us, in equal derivation (emanation), the yoga to be done is precisely the derivation that fully purifies all aspects”; by the third, the meaning of the foremost in outflow (derivation), by which, having understood the supremacy of the heard diffusion (emanation) of the <s>dharmadhātu</s>, for the sake of that he would cast himself even into a pit of fire measuring a three-thousand great-thousand world-system; by the fourth, the meaning of non-appropriation, for thus even thirst for Dharma (<s>dharmatṛṣṇā</s>) is turned back; by the fifth, the meaning of non-diversity of continuum, by means of ten equalities of the purification of mind and intention; by the sixth, the meaning of stainless purity, through the direct realization in dependent arising (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) that “there is no Dharma whatsoever that is defiled or purified”; by the seventh, the meaning of non-plurality, through signlessness, from the non-occurrence of plurality of signs of Dharma such as sūtra and so on; by the eighth, the meaning of non-loss and non-gain, from the attainment of the patience with the non-arising of Dharmas (<s>anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti</s>), because one sees no loss or increase of any Dharma in defilement or in purification,
182: The fourfold mastery (<s>vaśitā</s>): mastery of non-conceptuality, mastery of purity of fields, mastery of knowledge, and mastery of action; therein, the basis for the first two masteries is in the <s>dharmadhātu</s>, and it is precisely by the eighth bhūmi that it is penetrated; the basis for mastery of knowledge is on the ninth, through the attainment of discriminative knowledge (<s>pratisaṃvid</s>); the basis for mastery of action is on the tenth, through accomplishing the welfare of beings by creations (<s>nirmāṇa</s>) according to wish,
184: The obstruction of afflictions is taught, and likewise the obstruction of what is to be known; here, all obstructions—by the exhaustion of which liberation is maintained, II.17
185: For, by the exhaustion of this twofold obstruction, liberation from all obstructions is maintained,
186: [Āvaraṇapiṇḍārtha] The gist of the obstructions: the great obstruction is that which is pervasive; the thin obstruction is that which is localized; the obstruction of application is that which is excessive; the obstruction of attainment is that which is equal; the obstruction of distinctive attainment is that which lies in the absence of appropriation; the obstruction of right application is the ninefold obstruction of afflictions; the obstruction of cause is that which, beginning with the wholesome, pertains to the domain of the tenfold meanings of cause; the obstruction of entry into reality is that which is in the <s>bodhipakṣa</s>-factors; the obstruction of the unsurpassed wholesome is that which is in the <s>pāramitā</s>s; the obstruction of their distinctive course is that which is in the bhūmis; the obstruction of summary is that which, in summary, is twofold,
187: In the <s>Madhyāntavibhāga</s>, the section on obstruction is the second,
189: [CHAPTER III. TATTVAPARICCHEDA] With respect to reality (<s>tattva</s>), he says,
190: Reality characterized as root and as non-inversion,
191: Reality consisting of fruit-and-cause, and likewise subtle and coarse, III.1
192: Established, of the domain of purity, comprehensive, and of the mark of differentiation; the reality of skill, tenfold, opposed to the view of self, III.2
193: Thus this tenfold reality, namely: root-reality, mark-reality; non-inversion-reality; fruit-and-cause-reality; coarse-and-subtle-reality; established-reality; reality whose field is purity; comprehensive-reality; reality of subdivisions; and the reality of skill; and that, again tenfold, is to be understood by opposition to the tenfold grasping at self, as follows: the skill concerning aggregates; the skill concerning elements; the skill concerning sense-bases; the skill concerning dependent arising; the skill concerning what is a locus and what is not; the skill concerning faculties; the skill concerning paths (temporal stages); the skill concerning truths; the skill concerning vehicles; and the skill concerning the conditioned and the unconditioned,
196: The imagined, the other-dependent, and the perfectly accomplished; therein, because of the establishment of otherness of reality, what reality is maintained in this threefold nature?
198: Unreal and permanent, and real yet not of the nature of reality, and both real-and-unreal in respect of reality—thus the three natures are maintained, III.3
199: “The characteristic of the imagined (parikalpita) is permanent and unreal”—this is reality (<s>tattva</s>) in the <s>parikalpita</s>-nature, because of non-inversion; “the characteristic of the other-dependent (<s>paratantra</s>) is both real and not, not in respect of reality, because it is delusive”—this is reality in the <s>paratantra</s>-nature; “the characteristic of the perfectly accomplished (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>) is both real-and-unreal with respect to reality”—this is reality in the <s>pariniṣpanna</s>-nature,
201: Here, the seeing of superimposition and refutation regarding dharmas and persons (<s>pudgala</s>),
202: And also regarding the apprehended and the apprehender, and regarding existence and non-existence, III.4
203: That by whose cognition one would not proceed—that indeed is the mark of reality,
204: That, by whose cognition the seeing of superimposition and refutation with respect to persons and dharmas does not proceed—that is the mark of reality in the <s>parikalpita</s>-nature; that, by whose cognition the seeing of superimposition and refutation with respect to the apprehended and the apprehender does not proceed—that is the mark of reality in the <s>paratantra</s>-nature; that, by whose cognition the seeing of superimposition and refutation with respect to existence and non-existence does not proceed—that is the mark of reality in the <s>pariniṣpanna</s>-nature; this non-inverted mark, within root-reality, is what is called mark-reality,
205: [3. Non-inversion-reality] Non-inversion-reality (<s>aviparyāsatattva</s>): as the counteragent to the inversions beginning with permanence, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are, in root-reality, to be known in order; and how, there, are impermanence and the rest to be understood,
206: For the object of the unreal is the meaning of impermanence, characterized by arising and disintegration, III.5
207: In root-reality, in due order, by impurity and purity,
209: For the three natures are root-reality; among them, in due order,
210: The object of the unreal is the meaning of impermanence,
211: The meaning of arising-and-disintegration, and the meaning of impurity-and-purity,
212: Suffering is said, in another respect, to be characterized as the mark of appropriation; and in respect of relation, III.6
213: In root-reality, in due order, suffering is from appropriation—because of the appropriation that is the fixation on person and dharmas; as to mark, because its mark is the threefold suffering; and as to relation, because of relation to suffering; this, there itself in root-reality, is to be understood in due order,
214: And non-existence is also other-natured non-existence; its nature is said to be emptiness,
215: For the characteristic of the <s>parikalpita</s> does not exist in any way whatever—therefore its emptiness is precisely non-existence; for the characteristic of the <s>paratantra</s> does not exist as it is imagined, though it does not absolutely not exist—therefore its emptiness is other-natured non-existence; for the characteristic of the <s>pariniṣpanna</s> is precisely of the nature of emptiness—therefore its nature itself is emptiness,
216: And non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) is non-mark, and it is precisely that which is distinct from that, III.7
217: And its own-mark is also stated,
218: For the nature of the <s>parikalpita</s> has no mark at all—therefore its non-self is precisely non-mark; for the <s>paratantra</s> there is a mark, but not as it is imagined—therefore its non-self is the mark that is distinct from that; but the <s>pariniṣpanna</s>-nature is itself non-self—therefore its nature itself is non-self; thus, in the threefold root-reality, the threefold impermanence is made clear: the impermanence of the object that is unreal, the impermanence of arising-and-ceasing, and the impermanence of impurity-and-purity; the threefold suffering: suffering of appropriation, suffering as mark, and suffering as relation;
220: And the threefold emptiness: emptiness as non-existence, emptiness as other-natured non-existence, and emptiness as self-nature-emptiness; and the threefold non-self: non-self as non-mark, non-self as distinct-from-the-mark, and non-self as own-mark-non-self,
221: [4. Fruit-and-cause-reality] Fruit-and-cause reality (<s>phalahetumayatattva</s>): there itself, in root-reality, the truth of suffering, origination, cessation, and path; how is the threefold root-reality the truth of suffering and so on? Because it has the marks beginning with impermanence,
222: Therefore it is held to be the truth of suffering,
223: By the threefold sense of origination, it is the truth of origination; the three senses of origination are:
224: Disposition (<s>vāsanā</s>), and arisal, and also non-disjunction, III.8
225: Origination as disposition is the disposition of fixation on the <s>parikalpita</s>-nature; origination as arisal is action-and-afflictions (<s>karma</s>-<s>kleśa</s>); origination as non-disjunction is the non-disjunction of the veiling of suchness (<s>tathatā</s>); by the threefold cessation, it is the truth of cessation; the threefold cessation is:
226: The non-arising of the two natures, and what is called the twofold pacification of stains,
227: Non-arising of own-nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), non-arising of the apprehended and apprehender (<s>grāhya</s>-<s>grāhaka</s>), and the twofold pacification of stains (<s>mala-śānti-dvaya</s>)—this is called cessation through analytic discernment and suchness (<s>pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>-<s>tathatā</s>-designated); this is the threefold cessation, namely: cessation of own-nature, the twofold cessation, and natural (intrinsic) cessation (<s>prakṛti-nirodha</s>); how is the truth of path established within the threefold root-reality?
228: In full understanding and in abandonment, and in attainment and direct realization—this [is the way], III.9
230: The truth of path is thus declared,
231: By the full understanding of the imagined (<s>parikalpita</s>), and by the full understanding and abandonment of the other-dependent (<s>paratantra</s>); and by the full understanding and the making-manifest of attainment with respect to the perfectly accomplished (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>)—thus here, in the acts of full understanding, abandonment, and direct realization, the establishment of the truth of path is to be understood
232: [5. Coarse-and-subtle-reality] Coarse-and-subtle reality is again the conventional and the ultimate truth (<s>saṃvṛti</s>-<s>paramārtha</s>-satya); how is that to be understood within root-reality?
233: By designation and by practical attainment, and by elicitation it is coarse,
234: For the conventional is threefold: convention of designation (<s>prajñapti-saṃvṛti</s>), convention of practical attainment (<s>pratipatti-saṃvṛti</s>), and convention of elicitation (<s>udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti</s>); by that, conventional truth, within root-reality, is to be understood in due order
235: But the ultimate is from the one alone, III.10
236: Ultimate truth is to be understood from one own-nature only, namely from the perfectly accomplished (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>)—how, then, is that the ultimate?
237: For the ultimate is considered threefold by way of object, attainment, and practice
238: Object-ultimate is <s>tathatā</s> (suchness), taken as the object of supreme knowledge; attainment-ultimate is <s>nirvāṇa</s> (extinction), taken as the supreme aim; practice-ultimate is the path, taken as its supreme aim; how, then, is the perfectly accomplished own-nature said to be both the unconditioned and the conditioned?
239: By completion as non-modification and as non-inversion, the twofold [division arises], III.11
240: The unconditioned is perfectly accomplished by completion as non-modification; the conditioned, embraced by the truth of path, is, with respect to the knowable object, perfectly accomplished again by completion as non-inversion,
243: [6. Established-reality] How is established-reality to be set forth within root-reality? Established-reality is twofold: established by the world and established by reasoning; therein,
244: What is established by the world is from one [source],
245: namely from the imagined own-nature (<s>parikalpita-svabhāva</s>): in that existent, by a cognition imbued with conventional assignment and collective approval, there is a likeness of seeing for all worldlings; “this indeed is earth, not fire; this indeed is form, not sound,” and so forth,
246: What is established by reasoning is from the three,
247: namely: that existent which, relying on the three means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa-traya</s>), is established by the inferential proof of reasoning by the wise who are skilled in sound meaning, the logicians
248: [7. Domain-of-purification-reality] The domain-of-purification-reality is twofold: the domain of the knowledge of purification with respect to the obstruction of afflictions (<s>kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara</s>), and the domain of the knowledge of purification with respect to the obstruction of what is to be known (<s>jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara</s>); this
249: Domain-of-purification is proclaimed as twofold from the one alone, III.12
250: namely from the perfectly accomplished own-nature (<s>pariniṣpanna-svabhāva</s>) alone; for no other own-nature becomes the domain of the twofold knowledge of purification
251: [8. Comprehensive-reality] How is comprehensive-reality to be understood within the threefold root-reality?
252: There is a twofold comprehending, of mark (objective condition) and of conceptual construction, and also of name,
253: Beginning, as applicable, with the five things, there is, by the other-dependent (<s>paratantra</s>), a comprehending of mark and of conceptual construction; and of name, by the imagined (<s>parikalpita</s>)
256: And there is, of the reality of right knowledge alone, a single comprehending, III.13
257: namely, by the perfectly accomplished own-nature (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>) there is the comprehending of suchness and right knowledge
258: [9. Differentiated-reality] How is differentiated-reality to be understood within root-reality? Differentiated-reality is sevenfold: activity-reality, mark-reality, manifestation-reality, arrangement-reality, false-practice-reality, purification-reality, and right-practice-reality; and therein the triad beginning with activity-reality: “In the beginningless [stream], saṃsāra goes on; from the defilement of mind vis-à-vis <s>tathatā</s>, beings are defiled”—and likewise all the truth beginning with suffering, in due order; and moreover, in the <s>Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra</s>, the sevenfold suchness (<s>tathatā</s>) is taught; therein,
260: Root-reality is to be understood, as having the marks of the imagined and the other-dependent, just as [there is] activity-reality so also
262: even with respect to arrangement-reality and false-practice-reality, in just the same way there is a twofold root-reality,
263: one [more] is the right-practice of purity in respect of manifestation and of mark, III.14
264: The realities beginning with mark-reality are four; a single root-reality is the perfectly accomplished mark,
266: [10. Skill-reality] Skill-reality (<s>kauśalya-tattva</s>) is said to be by way of the antidote to views; how is there the tenfold self-view with respect to these [aggregates] beginning with the <s>skandhas</s>?
267: As [consisting in] unity, [as] causality, [as] enjoyership, [as] agenthood, [as] sovereignty,
268: as lordship, as having the meaning of permanence, and even as basis of defilement and of purification, III.15
269: as being a <s>yogin</s>, and as being unliberated-and-liberated—such is the seeing of self in these indeed,
270: This tenfold grasping of a non-existent self operates in the <s>skandhas</s> and so on; over against it, the tenfold skill is as follows, namely: the grasping of unity, the grasping of causality, the grasping of enjoyership, the grasping of agenthood, the grasping of independence, the grasping of overlordship, the grasping of permanence, the grasping that [takes them as] defiled-and-purified, the grasping of being a <s>yogin</s>, and the grasping of being both unliberated and liberated
271: How does this tenfold skill-reality fall within root-reality? Because the <s>skandhas</s> and the rest are included within the three natures; how are they included?
272: By the fact that, with respect to them, there is imagined, discriminated, and dharmatā-character, III.16
273: The threefold form: imagined form—namely, that which is the imagined own-nature of form; discriminated form—namely, that which is the other-dependent own-nature of form, for there, discrimination of form is effected; dharmatā-form—namely, that which is the perfectly accomplished own-nature of form; just as with form, so the <s>skandhas</s> beginning with feeling, and likewise the <s>dhātus</s> and <s>āyatanas</s>, are to be applied; thus, because the <s>skandhas</s> and so on are included in the three natures, the tenfold skill-reality is to be seen precisely within root-reality; this has been stated concerning the skill regarding the <s>skandhas</s> as the antidote to the tenfold self-view; but the object of the <s>skandhas</s> has not been stated—this now is stated
276: For the sake of the meanings of plurality, of summary, and of delimitation, first,
277: First of all, the <s>skandhas</s> are to be understood by a threefold meaning: by the meaning of plurality—namely, whatever form, whether past, future, or present, and so on in detail; by the meaning of summary—namely, all that is gathered into a unity in summary form; and by the meaning of delimitation—namely, because of the distinct determination of the mark of form and so on; for heap-meaning indeed is the very meaning of skandha, and thus in the world the heap-meaning is seen
279: Another [meaning] is taught: the meaning of apprehender, of apprehended, and of the seed of that apprehension, III.17
280: What is the other, the <s>dhātu</s>? Therein, the seed-meaning of the apprehender is the eye-<s>dhātu</s> and so on; the seed-meaning of the apprehended is the form-<s>dhātu</s> and so on; the seed-meaning of that apprehension is the eye-consciousness-<s>dhātu</s> and so on
282: Another [meaning is given] from the doors of knowing, delimitation of objects, and enjoyment,
283: What is the other, the <s>āyatana</s>? Therein, by the meaning of door for knowing and enjoying, the six internal <s>āyatanas</s>; and by the meaning of door for delimitation of objects and enjoying, the six external [<s>āyatanas</s>]
284: [d. Object of dependent arising] The object of dependent arising (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>),
285: Again—by way of the non-superimposition and non-denial of cause, fruit, and activity, III.18
286: The object of dependent arising is the meaning of non-superimposition and non-denial with respect to causes, fruits, and activities; therein, cause—there is non-superimposition, from rejecting the imagining of the conditioned factors such as formations as having disparate causes,
288: cause-negation is from imagining their being without cause; fruit-superimposition is from imagining that conditioned factors, which are with self, proceed by the condition that is ignorance and so on; fruit-negation is from imagining, “there are no conditions such as ignorance for formations and so on”; activity-superimposition is from imagining an operation for ignorance and so on in the production of formations and so on; activity-negation is from imagining their lack of capacity; by the absence of these, non-superimposition and non-denial are to be understood
289: [e. Object of what is fitting and unfitting]
290: Another [meaning is given] by way of the simultaneous arising and lordship of the undesirable, the desirable, and the pure; and by way of attainment, conventional practice, and dependence, III.19
291: What is fitting and unfitting (sthānāsthāna) is to be understood by the sevenfold meaning of dependence (<s>pāratantrya</s>): therein, in the undesirable there is dependence, because, even for one who does not wish it due to bad conduct, there is going to a bad destiny; in the desirable there is dependence, because from good conduct there is going to a good destiny; in purity there is dependence, because, without abandoning the five hindrances and without cultivating up to the seven factors of awakening, there is making an end of suffering; in simultaneous arising there is dependence, because, for the two unprecedented practitioners, namely a <s>Tathāgata</s> and a wheel-turning monarch (<s>cakravartin</s>), there is non-arising in a single world-system; in lordship there is dependence, because a woman does not effect wheel-turning-monarchy and so on; in attainment there is dependence, because a woman does not perfectly awaken to the individually-supreme unsurpassed awakening; in conventional practice there is dependence, because one possessed of view-attainment does not undertake procedures such as killing, whereas an ordinary person does undertake them—this should be followed out in detail in accordance with the Many-Factors Sūtra (<s>Bahudhātuka-sūtra</s>)
292: [f. The domain of the faculties (<s>indriyārtha</s>)] The faculty (<s>indriya</s>) moreover is of twenty-two kinds,
293: by the meanings of apprehension, of locus, of conjunction, of enjoyment, and of the twofold purity,
295: By the meaning of apprehension—up to by the meaning of the twofold purity—among these, because of their lordship therein: for, in the apprehension of objects such as form, there is lordship of the six beginning with the eye; in locus, there is the life-faculty’s lordship, because, through its authority, there is non-dying; in conjunction of family, there is the lordship of the female and male faculties, because of procreation of offspring; in enjoyment, there is the experience of the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma by the feeling-faculties; in worldly purity, those such as faith; in supramundane purity, those such as “I will know what has not been known” faculty,
297: Because of the meanings of fruit, cause, applicability, and non-applicability, thereafter another, III.20
298: What is the other, the threefold temporal series (<s>adhvatraya</s>)? As applicable, by the meaning of fruit-and-cause non-applicability, the past temporal series is to be understood; by the meaning of cause-applicability and fruit-non-applicability, the future temporal series; by the meaning of applicability of cause and non-applicability of fruit, the present temporal series
299: [h. The domain of the Four Truths (<s>catuḥsatyārtha</s>)]
300: By the meanings of feeling, sign of feeling, and attainment of that sign; by the fitness for the meaning of pacification and of antidote, another is approved, III.21
301: What is the other, the fourfold truth? Therein, the truth of suffering is by the meaning of feeling and of the sign of feeling—whatever is to be understood as “this here is of suffering,” making it thus; again, by “sign of feeling” the dharmas standing in the place of feeling are to be understood; by the attainment of that sign, the truth of origin, namely whatever attainment there is of the sign of the truth of suffering; of those two, by the meaning of pacification, the truth of cessation; by the meaning of antidote, the truth of path
302: [i. The domain of the three vehicles (<s>yānatrayārtha</s>)]
303: By knowledge discriminating qualities and faults with respect to nirvāṇa and <s>saṃsāra</s>, by what is heard from another or by oneself, and by going forth, another is to be known,
305: The three vehicles, as applicable: therein, by knowledge of the qualities and faults of <s>nirvāṇa</s> and <s>saṃsāra</s>, from another—having heard—and by the meaning of going forth, the <s>śrāvaka-yāna</s>; by that very [knowledge], without having heard oneself from another, by the meaning of going forth, the <s>pratyekabuddha-yāna</s>; by non-conceptual (<s>avikalpa</s>) knowledge, by oneself, by the meaning of going forth, the <s>Mahāyāna</s> is to be understood
306: [j. The domain of conditioned and unconditioned (<s>saṃskṛta-asaṃskṛtārtha</s>)]
307: From imputation, from cause, from sign, from pacification, from what has meaning, the last is set forth, III.22
308: Conditioned and unconditioned—therein, imputation (<s>prajñapti</s>) is name-aggregate and the like; cause is the store-consciousness (<s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>) that includes seeds; sign is what is included in the support-body and enjoyments; and grasping-up and conceptual construction included in the functioning consciousnesses—this complex of sign with associated factors, having imputation and cause, is to be understood as conditioned; therein, manas is that which constantly has the mode of conceiving, grasping-up is the fivefold consciousness-group, conceptual construction is mind-consciousness—because of its being conceptual, that is unconditioned? Rather, pacification (<s>praśama</s>) is cessation (<s>nirodha</s>); and the meaning of pacification is suchness (<s>tathatā</s>): there, taking pacification as cessation and path, and that by which there is pacification, making “meaning of pacification” to be suchness—the meaning of pacification—therefore, because suchness has the path as its support, and because the path has the character of pacification, therefore from pacification
309: By this meaning, knowledge regarding the <s>skandhas</s> and so on, and skill regarding the <s>skandhas</s> and so on, is to be understood
310: [Summary of the import of the realities] The gist of the realities (<s>tattvapiṇḍārtha</s>): in brief, the reality (<s>tattva</s>) is twofold: mirror-reality (<s>ādarśa-tattva</s>) and seen-reality (<s>dṛśya-tattva</s>); among these, mirror-reality is root-reality (<s>mūla-tattva</s>), because the remainder are seen by it,
312: ) Seen-reality is ninefold: seen-reality of non-conceit; seen-reality of non-inversion; seen-reality of going forth by the <s>Śrāvaka-yāna</s>; seen-reality of going forth by the <s>Mahāyāna</s>; seen-reality of refutation of opposing doctrines, through ripening by the gross and release by the subtle; seen-reality of refutation by reasoning, on the basis of reliance on examples; seen-reality of the illumination of the <s>Mahāyāna</s>; seen-reality of entry into the knowable in all modes (<s>sarvākāra-jñeya-praveśa</s>); seen-reality of the illumination of unfailing suchness (<s>avitatha-tathatā</s>); and also seen-reality of entry into all intentional engagements with respect to the real entity of self-grasping,
313: In the treatise <s>Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra</s>, the third [chapter] is the delimitation of reality (<s>tattva-pariccheda</s>)
315: [CHAPTER IV. Determination of the cultivation of the antidotes, the stages, and the fruits] [1. Cultivation of the antidotes] The cultivation of the antidote (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā</s>)—the cultivation belonging to the factors of awakening (<s>bodhipakṣya-bhāvanā</s>)—is now to be stated,
316: [a. The four establishments of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>)] Therein, first of all,
317: Because of coarseness, because of being the cause of thirst, because of being a real entity, and because of non-delusion, for the introduction to the Four Truths, there is the cultivation of the establishments of mindfulness, IV.1
318: For coarseness is made prominent by the body; by its examination the truth of suffering is entered, because it has the characteristic of being formed with perpetual coarseness; for coarseness is the painfulness-of-formations—by that the noble ones see all that is with outflows as of the nature of suffering; feeling is the cause of thirst—by its examination the truth of origin is entered; mind, the real entity of clinging to self, by its examination the truth of cessation is entered, due to the removal of the fear of annihilation of self; by the examination of dharmas, through non-delusion regarding defiled and purified dharmas, the truth of the path is entered therefore, to begin with, for the introduction to the Four Truths, the cultivation of the establishments of mindfulness is laid down,
319: [b. The four right abandonings (<s>samyak-prahāṇa</s>)] Then, the cultivation of right abandoning—for,
320: When the contrary and the antidote have been fully known in every way, energy for their removal indeed proceeds in four ways, IV.2
321: By the cultivation of the establishments of mindfulness, when the contrary and the antidote have been fully known in all modes, energy proceeds fourfold for the removal of the contrary and the approach of the antidote—namely, for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome dharmas, and so forth in detail,
324: When there is fitness of mind established there, for the accomplishment of all aims, through the abandoning of the five faults and the cultivation of the eight trainings, it follows, IV.3
325: When in that cultivation of energy for their removal there is stability of mind, there is fitness (<s>karmaṇyatā</s>): the four bases of success are set forth, because they are the cause of the accomplishment of all aims; here, “stability” of mind is to be understood as concentration (<s>samādhi</s>); therefore, after the right abandonings, [come] the bases of success; and that fitness, moreover, is to be understood as following upon the abandoning of the five faults and the cultivation of the eight trainings of abandoning,
326: [The five faults (<s>pañca doṣāḥ</s>)] Which are the five faults? He says:
327: Sloth (<s>kausīdya</s>), disparagement (<s>avavāda</s>), loss (forgetfulness) (<s>saṃmoṣa</s>), sinking (<s>laya</s>), excitement (<s>uddhata</s>), non-preparation (<s>asaṃskāra</s>), and then preparation (<s>saṃskāra</s>)—these five faults are considered, IV.4
328: Therein, sinking-and-excitement are taken as one fault; non-preparation is the fault at the time of not pacifying sinking and excitement; preparation is [a fault] at the time of pacification,
329: [The eight trainings for abandoning (<s>aṣṭa prahāṇa-saṃskārāḥ</s>)] For the abandoning of these, how are the eight trainings for abandoning established? Four are for the abandoning of sloth: zeal (<s>chanda</s>), energy (<s>vyāyāma</s>), faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), and pliancy (<s>prasrabdhi</s>)—and these are to be understood, further, in due order,
330: Support, and that which depends on the support, its sign, and the result as well,
331: The support is zeal; energy depends on the support; the sign of that support—of zeal—is faith, on the ascertainment, due to aspiration for the truth; the result of that dependent energy is pliancy, for one who has initiated vigor, because of the attainment of a special concentration,
333: The remaining four trainings for abandoning are mindfulness, clear comprehension, intention, and equanimity; these are, respectively, the antidotes to the four faults in due order; and again, those beginning with mindfulness should be understood in sequence,
334: Non-forgetfulness with respect to the object; the discerning of sinking and excitement; the formation (cultivation) for the removal of that; in pacification, smooth flowing-guidance—IV.5
335: Mindfulness is non-lapse with respect to the object; clear comprehension is the discerning of sinking and excitement when there is non-lapse of mindfulness; having discerned, intention is the formation (cultivation) for the removal of that; when there is pacification of that sinking and excitement, equanimity is the mind’s smooth flowing-guidance [ ]
336: [d. The five faculties (<s>pañcendriyāṇi</s>)] Immediately after the bases of success, the five faculties beginning with faith—how is their arrangement?
337: When the liberation-partaking wholesome root has been established, through the mastery of zeal and of application; and of non-forgetfulness with respect to the object; and of non-diffusion; and of investigation—IV.6
338: “Through mastery” continues in sense; when, by the bases of success, the liberation-partaking wholesome root has been established for a mind made fit, then through the mastery of zeal, through the mastery of application, through the mastery of non-lapse with respect to the object, through the mastery of non-diffusion, and through the mastery of investigation, the five faculties beginning with faith should be understood in order,
339: [e. The five powers (<s>pañca balāni</s>)] Those very [five], beginning with faith, being strong are called powers; as for their being strong,
340: It is indeed by scraping away (attenuation) of the adversary,
342: when those [faculties] are not scattered by adversaries such as disbelief; why is there a prior-and-later statement of those beginning with faith? Because
343: the later is the fruit of the former,
344: for one who has faith undertakes energy with respect to cause and fruit; for one who has undertaken energy, mindfulness becomes established; when mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, one knows things as they are; the faculties have been stated for the deposited (established) liberation-partaking [ground], so then, should the penetration-partaking be understood at the level of faculties, or at the level of powers?
345: Two and two of the penetration-partaking are faculties and powers—IV.7
346: The heat and the summit are faculties; the world-transcending forbearances and the supreme qualities are powers,
347: [f. The seven factors of awakening (<s>sapta bodhyaṅgāni</s>)] Immediately after the powers, the awakening-factors—how is their arrangement?
348: The basis-limb, the nature-limb, the exit-limb, the third; the fourth is the benefit-limb; the non-defilement-limb is taught as threefold—IV.8
349: On the path of seeing, the limbs for awakening are the factors of awakening; therein, mindfulness is the basis-limb of awakening; investigation-of-dharmas is the nature-limb; energy is the exit-limb; rapture is the benefit-limb; the non-defilement-limb is threefold: pliancy, concentration, and equanimity; why, again, is the non-defilement-limb taught as threefold?
351: It is taught here by way of cause, by way of basis, and by way of nature,
352: Pliancy is the cause of non-defilement, because coarseness is the cause of defilement; and concentration is the basis of that, since it is the antidote to it; in nature it is equanimity [ ]
353: [g. The eight factors of the path (<s>aṣṭa mārgāṅgāni</s>)] Immediately after the awakening-factors, the path-factors—how is their arrangement?
354: Discrimination, then attainment from others, and approving of others—threefold—IV.9; and the adversary–antidote as the limb of the path is eightfold,
355: On the path of cultivation, right view—worldly and supramundane, obtained subsequently—by which one discriminates one’s own realization—is the discrimination-limb; right intention and right speech are the attainment-from-others limb, because through speech along with its arousal that [attainment from others] is effected; the approving-of-others limb is threefold: right speech, right action, and right livelihood, because, respectively,
356: approval by others is admitted with regard to view, morality, and refinement,
357: for, through right speech, there is approval regarding wisdom by the determination in the discussion of discourses; through right action, regarding morality, by refraining from what ought not be done; through right livelihood, regarding refinement, by a righteous measure and by seeking robe and so on; the adversary–antidote limb is just threefold: right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; of these, in due order, there is
358: overcoming of afflictions and subsidiary afflictions, and being the antidote to adversaries,
359: for the adversary is threefold: the affliction to be abandoned by cultivation; the subsidiary affliction is sinking–and–excitement (
361: ) And the adversary of pervasion is the obstruction to the bringing forth of the distinguished qualities of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> [system]; there, for the first, right effort is the antidote, because of the cultivation of the path by it; for the second, right mindfulness, because, with mindfulness well established on the supports such as <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding), there is an absence of sinking and excitement; for the third, right concentration, because, relying on the absorptions (<s>dhyāna</s>), there is the bringing forth of such qualities as superknowledges (<s>abhijñā</s>),
362: [h. The divisions of the cultivation of the antidote (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā-prabheda</s>)] This cultivation of the antidote, in brief, is to be understood as threefold,
363: Favorable, inverted, accompanied by a sequel; inverted—IV.11
364: and non-inverted; and the cultivation not accompanied by the sequel,
365: Even the inverted is: inverted yet favorable to the non-inversion; inverted and accompanied by the inversion as sequel; non-inverted; and non-inverted without the sequel of inversion—these, in due order, in the states of the ordinary person, the learner, and the non-learner; but for the <s>bodhisattvas</s>,
366: the attainment of object and attention, and their being distinguished—IV.12
367: For the <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>, the aggregates beginning with body that belong to their own mental continuum are the object; for the <s>bodhisattvas</s>, the aggregates beginning with body that belong to their own and to others’ continua; the <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> attend to body and so on with modes such as impermanence; but the <s>bodhisattvas</s> by the discipline of non-apprehension; the <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> cultivate the establishments of mindfulness and so on only up to the disjunction from body and so on; the <s>bodhisattvas</s> not for disjunction, nor for non-disjunction, but only up to non-abiding nirvāṇa (<s>apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa</s>); thus the cultivation of the antidote has been stated,
369: [2. The states there] What is the state there?
370: It is named the state of cause, of descent; called application and fruit; and distinguished as what is to be done and what is not to be done; and higher and unsurpassed—IV.13
371: Also at decisive resolution, at entry, at going out, and at prediction,
372: at the condition of being a preacher, at consecration, at attainment, and at commendation—IV.14
373: the performance of the tasks is declared,
374: There, the state of cause is the state of the one in the lineage (<s>gotra</s>); the state of descent is the state of one who has produced the thought of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>); the state of application is after the production of mind, before the attainment of the fruit; the state of fruit is at attainment; the state of what is to be done is that of the learner; the state of what is not to be done is that of the non-learner; the state of distinction is that of one endowed with distinctions of qualities such as superknowledges; the higher state is that of a <s>bodhisattva</s> who has entered the grounds in distinction from <s>Śrāvakas</s> and so on; the unsurpassed state is that of a Buddha, because beyond that there is no state; the state of decisive resolution is, for <s>bodhisattvas</s>, on the entire level of conduct of decisive resolution; the state of entry is on the first ground; the state of going out is on the six grounds succeeding that; the state of prediction is on the eighth ground; the state of being a preacher is on the ninth; the state of consecration is on the tenth; the state of attainment is the <s>dharmakāya</s> of the Buddhas; the state of commendation is the enjoyment body (<s>sāṃbhogika-kāya</s>); the state of performance of the tasks is the emanation body (<s>nirmāṇa-kāya</s>); all this is to be understood along with many and various states,
375: Again, in the <s>dharmadhātu</s> there are three: impure, impure-pure, and pure; and, as appropriate, purified—IV.15
376: Therein, the impure state extends up to the state of cause and application; the impure-pure state (
378: ) is that of the learners; the purified state is that of the non-learners
379: The ordering of persons is to be understood accordingly
380: Therefore, from the divisions of state, the ordering of persons is to be understood accordingly—“this one is in the lineage,” “this one has descended,” and so on; the states have been stated
381: [3. Attainment of fruits] What is the attainment of fruits?
382: Vesselhood is called maturation; power, because of mastery over that—IV.16
383: Taste, increase, and purification—this is the fruit, in due order,
384: Vesselhood is that maturation which is favorable to the wholesome; power is the greater measure of the wholesome due to the mastery that comes from vesselhood; taste is the taste for the wholesome due to former practice; increase is the fostering of the wholesome roots due to practice of wholesome dharmas arisen in the present; purification is the removal of the coverings; this fivefold fruit, in due order, is to be understood as maturation-fruit, mastery-fruit, outflow-fruit, fruit of personal effort, and separation-fruit,
385: The first and each successive [fruit] up to completion, due to practice of that, successively—IV.17
386: Because of favorableness, and because of the adversary, on account of disjunction, and especially because of distinction; and because of higher and unsurpassed, the fruit is otherwise (i.e., is to be classified differently) in brief—IV.18
387: The higher-and-higher fruit, from the <s>gotra</s> (lineage) up to the production of mind (<s>cittotpāda</s>)—and so on—should be understood in succession; the initial fruit is, first, the obtaining of supramundane dharmas; the fruit of practice is, after that, in the learner’s state; the fruit of completion is the non-learner dharmas; the favorableness-fruit is to be understood, in the manner of an upaniṣad (inner ground/propinquity), precisely as the successive higher-and-higher fruit; the adversary-fruit is the path of abandonment—which indeed is the initial fruit—the intended antidote (<s>pratipakṣa</s>); the disjunction-fruit is the direct realization of cessation, and the disjunction from afflictions is both the fruit of practice and the fruit of completion, for learner and non-learner respectively
389: The distinction-fruit is the distinguished quality such as superknowledge (<s>abhijñā</s>); the higher fruit is the <s>bodhisattva</s> grounds, because of being higher than the other vehicles; and the unsurpassed fruit is the Buddha-ground; these four belong precisely to the subdivision of practice-fruit and completion-fruit—this is that “other” fruit, stated in brief; but in detail it is without limit
390: [Summary-meaning of the cultivation of the antidote (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā</s>)] There, the gist of the cultivation of the antidote: cultivation by way of derivation (analysis), cultivation by way of eradication of traces (non-inscription), cultivation by way of preparation; cultivation by way of the higher undertaking; conjoined cultivation, because of conjunction with the path of seeing; entered cultivation, excellent cultivation, initial cultivation, middle cultivation, final cultivation; cultivation with higher (sequel), and cultivation without higher (sequel), distinguished by object and by attention and by attainment. The gist of the states: the state of being capable (fit to be guided) is that of one established in <s>gotra</s>; the state of initiation is up to application; the impure state, the impure–pure state, the pure state; the ornamented state; the state of pervasion because of pervading the ten grounds; and the unsurpassed state. The gist of fruits, in summary, as to their distinctions, from prior practice, and by extraction in successive higher stages; by indication (heading) and by detailed statement: therein, in summary, there are five fruits; as to their distinctions, the remaining ones; from prior practice, the maturation-fruit (<s>vipāka-phala</s>); by extraction in successive higher stages, the other four; by indication, the four beginning with the higher-and-higher fruit; by detailed statement, the six beginning with the favorableness-fruit; by the detailed statement of just those four
393: In the Madhyāntavibhāga, the delineation of the stages, fruits, and states of the cultivation of the antidote is the fourth
395: [CHAPTER V. Delineation of the Unexcelledness of the Vehicles] [1. The threefold unexcelledness] Now the unexcelledness of the vehicles is to be stated; that is said
396: Unexcelledness is, to be sure, held with respect to practice, and again with respect to the object; unexcelledness by way of assemblage is taught
397: Threefold is the unexcelledness in the <s>Mahāyāna</s>: by which this vehicle is unexcelled—unexcelledness of practice; unexcelledness of object; and unexcelledness of assemblage
398: [2. Unexcelledness of practice] There, the unexcelledness of practice is to be understood from the practice of the ten <s>pāramitās</s>
401: In the highest (parama) and in attention, in the non-dharma, in the absence of the two extremes; the distinguished and the non-distinguished
402: Thus this sixfold practice, namely: the highest practice; the attention-practice; the non-dharma-practice; the practice devoid of the two extremes; the distinguished practice; and also the non-distinguished practice
